turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mrs Deshmukh? Please come in. I am Sister Meera. Doctor will be here shortly, but I will take your readings and see the dressing first.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, sister. Thank you. I hope I am not holding up the clinic. The baby was fussy, so we left the house a little late.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Not at all. How have you been since the operation? Sit comfortably, I will put the cuff on.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The caesarean was ten days back. For the first week the stitch line was quiet, more or less. Then the lower end became red, and there is a little discharge. Last night I also felt feverish.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): All right. Temperature now is 37.1. Blood pressure is 118 over 76. Pulse is 94. Oxygen saturation is 98 percent.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ninety-four does seem a bit fast. I have been walking about with the baby, so perhaps that is why. The pressure sounds lower than what they told me in the nursing home, but I will not argue with the machine.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Pulse can sit a little high after an operation, and with a new baby. I am going to take this dressing off now. It may pull.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Kindly go slowly, sister. The lower corner stings when the tape comes away.

[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): Dressing is off. The upper half is dry and closed, but the lower end is red, roughly three centimetres, and the gauze has a small amount of yellow discharge. I do not see the wound gaping, though it is sore when I press just there.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is the spot. It was not like this when they took the outer dressing off on day five.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, Mrs Deshmukh, I am Dr Rao. Sorry to keep you waiting. Sister has started us off. Tell me, in your own words, what has been worrying you.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. It is the operation wound itself. There is redness and some discharge, and I had fever yesterday night. I wanted you to kindly have a look before it becomes something bigger.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): I am glad you came in rather than waiting it out. When you say discharge, what does it look like, and when did you first notice it?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): It is yellow, a little sticky — not a large amount, doctor. I noticed it, well, actually the day before yesterday, when I was changing the pad. Or was it yesterday morning? I am sorry, the nights are all mixed up with the baby.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): That is quite all right. New babies do that to the calendar. And the redness — did that come along with the discharge, or earlier?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): It was a little pink earlier, I think, but I cannot put a date on it. The days run together, doctor. I am sorry I cannot be more exact.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): No need to apologise. Have you had pain in the wound itself?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. A dull ache at the lower end. More when I get up from the bed. It is not severe — more of a nagging, if that is the word.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does that pain travel upwards, towards the chest or the shoulder?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. It stays around the stitch line, I think. It is hard to be sure.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): We will leave that as unclear, then — no need to force it. Tell me about the fever. Was it only last night?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Only last night, doctor. I felt hot and a bit shivery around eleven. I took one Crocin, the 500 one, and by morning the fever had gone. I am not feeling hot now.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good that it settled. Any cough, any burning when you pass urine, any loose motions?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. No cough, no burning, and the motions are normal. No loose motions.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any bleeding from the wound, or a bad smell from that discharge?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No bleeding, doctor. And I have not noticed any smell.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): After the caesarean, which tablets did they send you home with?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): They gave me the antibiotic, Augmentin, and my iron tablets for the blood. I also have Crocin at home for pain or fever. I am not on the sugar tablets anymore — they stopped those once the baby came.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the Augmentin. How much were you taking, and for how many days?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): It was one tablet in the morning and one at night. The course was five days... or was it seven? Um, I am not very sure. I finished whatever was in the packet.
[SEG0031] person_1 (NURSE): On the discharge slip from the nursing home it is written Augmentin 625 milligrams, one tablet twice daily, for five days.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): 625? I am sorry, sister, I thought the strip said 375. Perhaps I misread it. And the days — five days, or was it seven? I still cannot say. My husband threw the cover away.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then we will not pretend the dose is settled. I will note that the slip and your memory do not match. Are you still taking the iron tablets every day?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor, one iron tablet every morning, after food. They said my blood was low in the pregnancy, and it is still a little low, so I have continued.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): And those sugar tablets — do you remember the name at all?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I am afraid I do not. They were small white tablets, for the sugar in pregnancy. I stopped them the day after the delivery, as the obstetrician said. I have not been checking sugars at home.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to medicines, or to anything else, that you know of?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. No allergy that I know of.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sister, may I look as well? I would like to see that lower end myself.
[SEG0040] person_1 (NURSE): Of course. I have not cleaned it yet, so you can see the discharge as it is.

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Yes — redness at the lower end, a little yellow discharge, and the edges are still together. There is no gap, and nothing I can feel as a collection of pus. It is tender, just as you found.

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): I am turning this over in my mind, and I will not rush it. It may be an early wound infection, or it may only be a reaction to the stitches. The yellow discharge at the lower end pushes me towards infection, but I will not conclude that it is deep and I am not calling it an abscess today. The swab has to come back before I say more than that.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand, doctor. Will I need another operation? Please tell me plainly.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not from what I see today. No opening of the wound, and no drainage. We will swab it, change the antibiotic, and watch you closely.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): That is a relief. My mother-in-law was very worried and wanted turmeric on it. I did not do that. I only kept the pad on.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): You were right not to put turmeric or oil on it. Keep the area clean and dry, wash your hands before you touch it, and we will put a light dry dressing back on. If the redness spreads quickly, or the fever comes back, or the discharge becomes heavy, come sooner and do not wait.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): I can take the swab now and then redress it, if you want that done today.

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, please. Wound swab for culture today. I will also ask for a full blood count and a CRP, just to see the response. I am not going to read a diagnosis into those numbers until they are back.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the blood test be today itself? I have to get back for the baby's feed.

[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, today, here. It will not take long. Augmentin has had its course, and I do not want to repeat the same one while the slip and your strip do not agree. I will switch you to cephalexin, 500 milligrams, by mouth, twice a day, for five days.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Twice a day, for five days. Should I take it after food, doctor?

[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, after food, with water. Finish all five days even if the wound looks better. Continue the iron tablet as you are. You may take Crocin 500 milligrams, up to three times a day, if the pain or fever returns — not more than that.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. I will write it down so I do not mix the days again. Five days of the new one. The old course I still cannot swear to.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Please do write it down. I want to see you again in two days, wound and all, even if you feel well. The swab may not be reported by then, but I still want a look.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): In two days. Should I come even if there is no fever?
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, come either way. And if the redness spreads or the fever returns before that, do not wait for the two days — come straight in.
[SEG0057] person_1 (NURSE): I will book her for Thursday, doctor, and I will do the swab and the dry dressing once you are done. The bloods I can send with the porter.

[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday is all right. My husband can drive me. The baby is feeding well, by the way — that part has been a blessing. I was more frightened about the wound than about myself, if that makes sense.

[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): It makes complete sense, and I am happy the baby is feeding. You did the right thing by coming. We will see you in two days, sooner if things change. Sister will finish the swab and the dressing now.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. You have been very kind. I will finish the new tablets and keep the wound dry.

[SEG0061] person_1 (NURSE): I will just clean around it gently, take the swab from the yellow area, and put a dry gauze on. You may hold the baby after that. If the sting is too much, tell me and I will pause.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Please go ahead, sister. I will manage. Thank you both.

spec.situation: Patient 10 days after a hernia, appendix or caesarean operation; wound redness and discharge, fever the night before; nurse removes dressing and describes it; patient is vague about antibiotic course ('five days... or was it seven'); wound swab and antibiotic change.
features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

bad.reason: Supported for redness spreads or fever returns; discharge becomes heavy is omitted.
bad.text: consultation (time_reference=value: if the redness spreads or the fever returns, status=conditional)

omissions.text: Negative finding asked and answered: wound pain does not clearly travel upward; patient thought it stays around the stitch line, and the doctor explicitly left radiation as unclear rather than present.
Examination finding by the doctor missing: wound edges are still together / no wound gap.
Follow-up advice was broader than recorded: return sooner not only if redness spreads or fever returns, but also if the discharge becomes heavy.
Timing/booking detail missing from follow-up: nurse booked the review for Thursday.
Investigation timing detail missing: the doctor said the blood test would be done today, here.
